label: Contact Forms
notes: This lecture opens the odd-dimensional half of the course. Where symplectic geometry lives on even-dimensional manifolds, contact geometry lives on dimension two n plus one and replaces the symplectic form with a maximally non-integrable hyperplane field. Stress that the whole subject is governed by a single nonvanishing condition we will meet on the next slide.

label: The Contact Condition
notes: Define a contact form as a one-form whose top wedge product is a volume form. Emphasise that alpha wedge d-alpha to the n must be nowhere zero, an open and pointwise condition. Contrast this with merely defining a plane field: any nonvanishing one-form does that, but only contact forms force the planes to twist.

label: Maximal Non-Integrability
notes: Connect the volume condition to Frobenius. An integrable plane field admits integral surfaces, but the contact condition is exactly the strongest failure of integrability in odd dimensions. Walk through the R3 model, computing the bracket of the two spanning fields and showing alpha evaluated on it is nonzero, so the bracket escapes the distribution.

label: The Standard Form on R^{2n+1}
notes: Present the Darboux normal form. Every contact structure looks locally like the standard one, so this single model carries all local information. Compute that alpha wedge d-alpha to the n equals the Euclidean volume form for the standard coordinates, confirming the model is genuinely contact and giving students a concrete formula to anchor intuition.

label: Twisting Planes in R^3
notes: Spend time on the picture. As x increases the second spanning vector tips downward, rotating the contact plane about the x-axis. No surface can stay tangent to this rotating family, which is the visual meaning of non-integrability. Point to the integrable comparison ker dz where the planes stay flat and surfaces exist.

label: The Reeb Vector Field
notes: Introduce the Reeb field as the canonical direction transverse to the contact planes. Its two defining equations pin it uniquely: it lies in the kernel of d-alpha and is normalised by alpha of R equals one. Note that the Reeb field depends on the chosen form, not only on the contact structure, and its flow generates contact dynamics.

label: Conformal Ambiguity
notes: Explain that the contact structure is the kernel, not the particular form. Replacing alpha by f alpha for a nowhere-zero f leaves the planes unchanged and rescales the contact volume by f to the n plus one, which stays nonzero. This conformal freedom is why Gray's theorem carries an extra scalar factor and why the Reeb field is not intrinsic.

label: Examples
notes: Survey the standard examples. The unit cotangent bundle and unit sphere bundle carry the contact form from the tautological one-form restricted to the unit level. The one-jet space of functions on X is contact with alpha equal to dz minus the canonical sum. These examples recur throughout the rest of the course.

label: Contact Elements
notes: Describe a contact element as a point together with a tangent hyperplane, equivalently a covector kernel up to scale. The projectivised cotangent bundle is the space of all contact elements and carries a canonical contact structure with local form dx1 plus xi dx2. This makes the homework's contact-element language precise without quoting it.

label: The Symplectization
notes: Build the symplectization as the cone M times R with the two-form d of e-to-the-t alpha. Verify it is symplectic exactly when alpha is contact: the top power reproduces the contact volume times an exponential factor. This functor turns contact questions into symplectic ones and underlies much of the deeper theory.

label: Gray Stability
notes: State Gray's theorem as the contact analogue of Moser stability. A smooth family of contact structures on a closed manifold is carried by an ambient isotopy. The proof solves a Moser equation inside the moving hyperplane field, using nondegeneracy of d-alpha there, and records a conformal factor because only the kernel must be preserved.

label: Recap
notes: Recapitulate the chain of ideas: hyperplane field, the volume condition, maximal non-integrability, the standard model, the Reeb field, examples, and the symplectization. Stress that contact geometry is symplectic geometry shifted by one dimension, and preview that the next lectures exploit the symplectization and Reeb dynamics in earnest.
